Tiglath-pileser
TIG-lath-py-LEE-zer
n. (the Assyrian king who first carried Israel into captivity)
Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra, "my trust is in the son of Esharra," the god Ninurta; rendered in the KJV as Tiglathpileser and, once, Tilgathpilneser.

Biblical Definition

Tiglath-pileser III is the Assyrian king under whom the LORD’s judgment on the northern kingdom began in earnest. In the days of Pekah, he “took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria” (2 Kings 15:29), the opening act of the deportation that would end the ten tribes’ independent existence within a generation. His deeper entanglement with Judah is a case study in the folly of unbelief: when Syria and Israel combined against wicked King Ahaz, Ahaz refused the LORD’s own offer of a sign through Isaiah (Isaiah 7:10–12) and instead “sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me” (2 Kings 16:7), stripping the temple treasury to pay the price. Assyria came — and stayed, a permanent and eventually fatal presence in Judah’s affairs. Ahaz then traveled to Damascus to meet his new overlord and there saw a pagan altar he was so taken with that he had its pattern copied for the LORD’s own house (2 Kings 16:10). The Chronicler names the same king by his fuller Assyrian title, Tilgathpilneser, and states plainly that it was the LORD Himself, not mere geopolitics, who “stirred up the spirit” of this pagan king to carry the Transjordan tribes away (1 Chronicles 5:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Tiglath-pileser; he is the Assyrian king who first deported the northern tribes and whom King Ahaz hired against Syria and Israel, at the cost of the temple treasury and Judah's independence.

expand to see more

TIGLATH-PILESER, n. A king of Assyria who deported the northern tribes of Israel and was later hired by King Ahaz of Judah.

ASSYRIA, n. An ancient and powerful empire of the Mesopotamian region, the instrument of the LORD's judgment on the northern kingdom.

CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner or held in bondage; in Scripture, especially the exile of Israel and Judah for covenant unfaithfulness.

TRIBUTE, n. A stated sum or other valuable thing paid by one ruler or nation to another, in acknowledgment of submission.

APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of one's professed principles or faith; Ahaz's turning to pagan Assyria and a pagan altar pattern is a case study.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 15:29 — "In the days of Pekah king of Israel came Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and took Ijon, and Abelbethmaachah, and Janoah, and Kedesh, and Hazor, and Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and carried them captive to Assyria."

2 Kings 16:7 — "So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, saying, I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me out of the hand of the king of Syria, and out of the hand of the king of Israel, which rise up against me."

2 Kings 16:10 — "And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof."

1 Chronicles 5:26 — "And the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, and the spirit of Tilgathpilneser king of Assyria, and he carried them away, even the Reubenites, and the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, and brought them unto Halah, and Habor, and Hara, and to the river Gozan, unto this day."

Modern Corruption

A pagan Assyrian king whose deportation records match, in name and campaign, the Assyrians' own royal inscriptions is inconvenient for any theory that the historical books are late, unreliable legend.

expand to see more

Minimalist Old Testament criticism, quick to treat the kings' narratives as tendentious later composition, is quietest exactly where the evidence is strongest: extra-biblical Assyrian annals independently name Tiglath-pileser III's western campaigns, his reception of tribute from a king named Jehoahaz of Judah (Ahaz's fuller throne name), and his deportations from the very regions 2 Kings 15:29 lists. The convergence of an ancient pagan empire's own boasting inscriptions with Israel's inspired history is not the pattern a late, careless legend produces.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Isaiah's own commentary on this exact king: Ahaz, offered a sign as deep as hell or as high as heaven and refusing to ask (Isaiah 7:11–12), hired the very empire that would become “the rod of mine anger” (Isaiah 10:5) against his own house. Unbelief that will not trust the LORD's word inevitably trusts something else, and the something else always proves a harder master than the trouble it was hired to solve.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra, my trust is in the son of Esharra; Hebrew golah (H1473), captivity, exile; ebed (H5650), servant; ma'al (H4604), trespass, unfaithfulness.

expand to see more

Akkadian Tukulti-apil-Esharra — my trust is in the son of Esharra, the god Ninurta.

Hebrew golah (H1473) — captivity, the exiled company; the fate Tiglath-pileser began for Israel.

Hebrew ebed (H5650) — servant; Ahaz's own self-description to the Assyrian king.

Hebrew ma'al (H4604) — trespass, unfaithfulness; the Chronicler's verdict on the deported tribes (1 Chronicles 5:25).

Hebrew ur (H5782) — to stir up, arouse; the verb of the LORD stirring the king's own spirit.

Usage

"“Carried them captive to Assyria” — the beginning of the northern exile."

"“I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me” — Ahaz's fatal appeal."

"“The God of Israel stirred up the spirit of... Tilgathpilneser” — the LORD's sovereignty over a pagan king."
